steps.say: Is a whale a fish? No, a whale is a mammal. That answer came from a transformer running under MS-DOS.

steps.caption: Wrong twice, with full confidence
steps.say: So did this one: seventeen times twenty-three is ninety-six. It isn't.

scenes.headline: A transformer in 640 KB
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Doskey. Tiny is a small GPT that fits next to DOS in conventional memory. Its tricks are the same ones modern runtimes use.

steps.say: There is no tokenizer. Every printable character is a token, so the whole vocabulary is ninety-seven entries.
Each letter gets a token embedding plus a learned position, out of a context of 128.
Four layers of attention and a small ReLU block, with RMS norms and no biases.
The output reuses the token embedding, so one table does two jobs.
Then it picks a letter, and feeds it back in. Every answer letter is a full pass.

scenes.title: Bytes in memory, floats in the math

steps.term: Per-row scale: one float for each row of bytes
steps.say: Weights are signed bytes. But the sum is a float, so the multiply-add runs on the math coprocessor.
The row's scale is applied once, after the dot product. That is why it wants a 486DX, and crawls on an SX.

scenes.title: Three answers in DOSBox-X, 25,000 cycles
scenes.note: seconds of emulated time, my run
scenes.say: I ran it in DOSBox-X. Three answers took under a minute with the coprocessor. With it switched off, the software emulator took about thirty-one times as long.

scenes.title: Where the 540 KB goes, in bytes
scenes.say: Add it up. The weight file, an eight-bit cache of keys and values, and the program. That is most of the five hundred and forty kilobytes the README asks for.

scenes.title: A voice from one square wave

params.one: The PC speaker: one pitch, on or off
params.vowel: A vowel: two pitches, swapped every 2 ms
params.hiss: A hiss: a new random pitch every millisecond
params.word: A word: buzzes, hisses and clicks in a row

steps.say: And it talks. The PC speaker can play one square wave, at one pitch, and nothing else.

steps.term: Formants: the two pitches that make a vowel
steps.say: So for a vowel, it flips between two pitches every two milliseconds, and your ear blurs them together.
S and F become hiss, a new random pitch every millisecond. P and T are a tiny click.
String those together with the rhythm of speech, and you get a film robot.

items.say: On questions it never saw, it gets sixty-one percent right.
Its arithmetic stops at small sums and the twelve times table.

items.text: Makes things up outside its facts
items.say: Outside its facts, it invents answers with full confidence.

scenes.text: Store in bytes, compute in floats, quantize the cache, count every byte.
scenes.say: The model is a toy. The engineering is not: store in bytes, compute in floats, quantize the cache, and count every byte.

recap: int8 weights, float math, a DX
A vowel is two pitches, swapped
scenes.say: Letters as tokens, bytes for weights, and a vowel made of two pitches. Thanks for watching!
